blocks.prompt: The Blue That Is Not There
blocks.text: Here is something strange about the peacock. His famous fan is not his tail. Those long feathers grow from his back, just above the tail. Scientists call them the train. His real tail is short and plain and brown. It sits behind the train, and when the peacock wants to show off, the little brown tail pushes the whole train up like a hand pushing open a fan. The train holds about two hundred feathers. Most of them end in a bright spot called an eyespot. When the fan opens, a peahen sees a wall of eyes looking back at her. Now look closer at the color. There is no blue paint in a peacock feather. There is no green paint either. The only color inside is brown. The blue and the green and the gold are made of light. Each feather is covered in tiny rows of rods, packed tighter than you can see. The rows bounce some colors of light back to your eye and let the rest sink in. Move your head and the color moves too. Grind up a peacock feather and the shine is gone. All you have left is brown dust.

blocks.prompt: The Fan That Shivers
blocks.text: A peacock does not just stand there with his train open. He shakes it. If you watch, you can see the whole fan shivering. He does this about twenty five times every second, which is far too fast for you to count. And here is the surprising part. When scientists filmed the display with high speed cameras and slowed it down, they found that the eyespots barely move at all. The feathers around the eyespots are loose and hairy, so they blur and shimmer. The eyespots hold nearly still inside that shimmer, like a hundred steady eyes floating in a moving field. The rattle makes sound too, and not only the sound you can hear. Some of it is infrasound, a pitch so low that human ears miss it completely. Peahens can sense it. So a peahen standing in the grass nearby is being watched, shown, and rattled at, all at once, by a bird she may not even be looking at. And she is choosy about where she looks. Researchers fitted peahens with tiny eye tracking cameras to record what they actually stared at. The peahens spent most of their time looking at the bottom of the train, near the peacock's feet, not at the grand tip of the fan at all. Then, when the breeding season ends, the whole train falls out. Every long feather drops. For months the peacock walks around looking almost ordinary, and people collect the feathers off the ground. By the next breeding season he has grown the entire display again.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.
The Feather That Made Darwin Sick
blocks.text: In 1860, Charles Darwin wrote a letter to a friend and admitted that one thing was ruining his sleep. Not his critics. A feather. He wrote that the sight of a feather in a peacock's tail made him sick. The problem was that his own theory said it should not exist. Natural selection keeps what helps an animal survive. A five foot fan of shimmering feathers does not help a bird survive. It is heavy, it is slow to fold, and it announces the bird's position to every tiger and dog in the district. By Darwin's own logic, peacocks should have been eaten out of existence long ago. His answer, published eleven years later, was that survival is not the only test. An animal also has to reproduce, and if peahens prefer long trains, then long trains will spread through the population even if they shorten the peacock's life. He called this sexual selection. The peahen's taste is a force of nature, as real as a drought or a predator. Later biologists pushed the idea further. Perhaps the cost is not a side effect. Perhaps the cost is the whole message. Any weak bird can grow a few dull feathers, but only a genuinely healthy peacock, well fed and free of parasites, can afford to drag two hundred of them around all summer and still outrun a dog. The train is expensive precisely so that it cannot be faked. This is called the handicap principle. There is evidence for it. In one long study in an English park, researchers counted the eyespots on each peacock's train and recorded which males the peahens chose. Males with more eyespots mated more often. When the researchers trimmed eyespots off some trains, those males were chosen less. The peahens were counting, or doing something very much like counting. But science is not tidy. A seven year study in Japan followed a different peafowl population and found no such preference at all. The peahens there seemed to ignore the train entirely. So either peahens differ from place to place, or the eyespots matter less than everyone assumed, or there is something in the display we still have not measured. Darwin's feather has not finished making people uncomfortable.

notes: Structural color: melanin rods in a photonic lattice
One pigment only, and it is brown
The train is upper tail coverts, not tail feathers

blocks.prompt: Two Hundred Eyes, and Not a Drop of Blue
blocks.text: Pull one feather from a peacock's train and hold it up to the window. It is blue and green and bronze, and the colors slide across each other as you turn it. Now put that feather in a mortar and grind it to powder. The powder is brown. Not blue, not green. Brown. That is the first thing to understand about a peacock. Almost nothing you can see on it is a color in the ordinary sense. The feather contains one pigment, melanin, the same dull brown that darkens human hair. Everything else is architecture. Inside each tiny barbule, rods of melanin are stacked in a precise lattice, spaced roughly a hundred and fifty nanometers apart. Light striking that lattice is reflected back in overlapping waves. Waves of one wavelength reinforce each other and reach your eye as brilliant blue. Waves of every other wavelength cancel and vanish. Change the spacing of the rods by a few nanometers and the same feather returns green instead, or bronze, or a coppery yellow. The peacock is not painted. It is built, and the light does the rest. This is why the color shifts as you move: you are changing the angle, and the angle is the whole trick. The second thing to understand is that the display is not a tail. The train grows from the bird's back, from feathers called upper tail coverts, which on an ordinary bird are the short feathers that tidily cover the base of the tail. On a peacock they have run away with themselves, reaching a length and a number that make up more than half the bird's length. The real tail is behind: about twenty stiff, brown, unremarkable feathers whose job is to swing forward and hold the enormous train upright, like a stagehand propping up scenery. And it does not cost what everyone assumed. The obvious story is that a peacock pays for its beauty with its safety, hauling a heavy banner that must slow it down and get it killed. When a biologist finally tested this properly, filming peafowl taking off with high speed cameras and then repeating the test on birds whose trains had been removed, the difference in takeoff performance was too small to measure. The train, for all its size, is mostly air and thin barbs. It weighs about three hundred grams on a bird of five kilograms. The handicap may be real, but it is not the crude physical burden the story always claimed. The strangeness runs deeper than the Indian bird. In 1936, an American ornithologist named James Chapin was working in a museum in Belgium when he noticed two mounted birds in a dusty corner, mislabeled as young Indian peafowl. They were nothing of the kind. Chapin had already spent more than twenty years puzzling over a single odd feather he had taken from a Congolese man's headdress, unable to match it to any known species. The museum birds matched. He had found the Congo peafowl, a large African bird that no scientist had described, sitting stuffed on a shelf the whole time. The peacock is a good lesson in looking twice. The tail is not a tail. The blue is not blue. The burden may not be a burden. And a species can hide for two decades inside a single feather in a headdress.
